analytic.title: Predicting the Response Time of OPSFi-style Production Systems *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper focuses on the response time analysis problem: the problem of determining a priori the mazimal response time or response time upper bound of a given program. We study this problem in the context of OPS5 production systems. The response time of a program is investigated in two respects: the m uimal number of rule firings and the maximal number of basic comparisons made by the Rete network during the execution. The execution of a program always terminates in bounded time i f this program satisfies one of certain conditions. We present four of these wnditions for OPS5 production systems. An algorithm used to compute an upper bound on the number of rule firings is given. Furthermore, to have a better idea on the time required during the execution, we present an algorithm to compute the maximal time required during the match phase in terms of the number of wmparisons made by the Rete network.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Given a program p, the response time analysis problem is to determine the maximal response time or response time upper bound of p. We study this problem in the context of OPS5 [5] production systems. The response time of a program is measured in two respects: the number of rule firings and the number of basic comparisons made by the Rete network during the execution. Although the response time analysis problem is in general undecidable, there exist several classes of production systems for which the property of termination is guaranteed. per bound, if possible. The Potential Instantiation graph, showing the potential rule triggering patterns, is defined as the basis to classify OPS5 programs. We show that a program has a bounded response time if its Potential Instantiation graph is acyclic. A response time upper bound algorithm is then presented. Since it is well-known that the match phase consumes about 90% of the execution time, we present a strategy to compute the maximal number of comparisons made by the corresponding Rete network. F'urthermore, several classes of programs with cyclic Potential Instantiation graphs have been found to have bounded response times.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 overviews related research. Section 3 gives a brief review of OPS5 production systems. Section 4 investigates the class of programs with acyclic Potential Instantiation graphs. The response time upper bound algorithms are introduced. Section 5 investigates the programs with cyclic Potential Instantiation graphs. Finally, Section 6 concludes this paper.

div.head: Related research
div.p: Abiteboul and Simon [l] discuss the property of termination in the context of Datalog and show that this property is in general undecidable. Lark et al [7] consider the design and implementation issues in the development of the Lockheed Pilot's Associate system. They advocate using experimentation and analysis to guarantee timeliness by requiring the application programmer to set an upper bound on .process duration by extensive experimentation but do not show how to verify that the system will satisfy this upper bound.

div.head: Aiken et al [2]
div.p: presents a static analysis method for determining whether arbitrary sets of database production rules satisfy certain properties, including termination. Some conditions that guarantee the property of termination are introduced. However, they do not provide an algorithm for obtaining an execution time (or execution time upper bound) for a set of rules which is found to have the property of termination.

Barachini et al [3] advocate the use of a run-time prediction method for soft real-time systems. Barachini [4] presents three run-time prediction methods to evaluate the time required for actions in the righthand-sides of rules to be carried out. The time required by the Rete network, when a token is passed to it, is estimated. He shows that run-time prediction of interrupt-driven expert systems can be performed with finer granularity such as in action level. However, in his opinion, the prediction of the system as a whole is not achievable in a tractable manner.

div.head: OPS5 production systems
div.p: An OPS5 [5] production system consists of three major components:

The working memory (WM) serves as a global database. Each entry in the working memory is called a working memory element (WME) r e p resenting a fact/assertion of the application domain. Each working memory element consists of a number of fields, each of which represents an attribute of the fact/assertion. A working memory element is classified as an old WME if it exists at the invocation; otherwise, it is a new WME, resulting from a rule firing. 0 The production memory (PM) consists of a set of rules called productions. Each production contains a condition part, called the left-hand side (LHS), and an action part, called the right-handside (RHS). The condition part is a conjunction of patterns, called condition elements. A condition element is matched by a working memory element if their corresponding fields are matched. Let cf denote the ith non-negated condition element of r. The WMEs matching cf are called the matching WMEs of cf. A WME is a matching WME of r if it is a matching WME of a non-negated condition element of r . A non-negated condition element is satisfied if it is matched by a working memory element. A negated condition element is satisfied if it cannot be matched by any working memory element.

The LHS of a production is matched if all of its condition elements are satisfied. A production is instantiated if its LHS is matched. An instantiation of a production is created if this production is instantiated. A production may have multiple instantiations at the same time. The action part is a sequence of command(s), called action(s), to be carried out when the rule is fired. 0 The inference engine repeatedly carries out the recognize-act cycles until a halt action is performed or no rule can be instantiated. Each recognize-act cycle consists of three phases: match All of the instantiations are found and stored in a set called conflict set. The Rete algorithm [6] is used in this phase. select Based on the adopted conflict resolution strategy, one of the instantiations in the conflict set is selected. fire The actions of the selected instantiation are carried out.

The execution of a program terminates when the process of recognize-act cycles stops. The response time (execution time) in this paper is measured in two respects: the number of recognize-act cycles (rule firings) carried out and the number of comparisons made by the Rete network during the execution.

Since there cannot be more rule firings than the number of instantiations that exist during the execution, the maximal number of instantiations that exist during the execution is an upper bound on the number of rule Sings. Based on this fact, we present a response time upper bound algorithm, which counts the maximal number of instantiations. The response time upper bound obtained by applying this algorithm to an initial working memory consisting of the maximal possible number of WMEs is a response time upper bound of the system, since all of the executions cannot have a larger number of WMEs than the (already known) maximal possible number of WMEs. An advantage of this algorithm is that the upper bound obtained is independent of the resolution strategy used.

div.head: Match time
div.p: In this section, we compute an upper bound on the number of comparisons made by the Rete algorithm [SI. Each comparison is a basic testing operation such as testing whether the value of the attribute ?Age is greater than 20, etc.

div.head: The Rete network
div.p: The Rete network receives as input the changes to the working memory and produces as output the modifications to the conflict set. The descriptions of the working memory changes are called tokens. A token consists of a tag and a working memory element. The tag of a token is used to indicate the addition or deletion of the working memory element of the token. We say a token is of the class a if the working memory element of the token is of the class a.

Each Rete network has a root node and several terminal nodes. The root node distributes to other nodes the tokens which are passed to the network. The terminal nodes are nodes each of which reports the satisfaction of the LHS of some rule. Other than the root node and terminal nodes, there are two types of nodes in the Rete network: one-input nodes and two-input nodes. Each one-input node tests for the presence of one intra-element feature, while each two-input node tests the inter-element feature(s) applying to the elements it processes. The intra-element features are the ones each of which involves only one working memory element. The inter-element features are the conditions involving more than one working memory element.

Those one-input nodes which receive tokens from the root node are called class-checking nodes, since they check the classifications of tokens. When a token is passed to the network, the root node distributes a copy of this token to each of the class-checking nodes. Each two-input node maintains a list, called L-list, of tokens coming from its left input and a list, called R-list, of tokens coming from its right input. The right-inputs of two-input nodes always receive tokens from one-input nodes. For more details about the Rete network, the reader is referred to [SI.

div.p: Let IEp denote the corresponding Rete network of the program p. When a token of the class a is passed to Rp, only one of the class-checking nodes accepts this tokenthe one requesting the token class be aand continues the process of token-passing. New token(s) may be generated and passed during the process. The thread of token-passing continues until the token is discarded or received by a terminal node which reports the satisfaction of some rule. All of the descendants of the satisfied class-checking node may accept all of the new tokens generated in the worst case.
Since each one-input node tests for the presence of one intra-element feature, one comparison is conducted whenever a token is passed to a one-input node.

On the other hand, a two-input node may conduct many comparisons, since many pairs of tokens may have to be checked whenever a token is passed to this node. Each pair of tokens consists of the incoming token and one of the tokens in the maintained list corresponding to the other input. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The response time analysis problem of production systems is rarely discussed, mainly due to the fact that it is in general undecidable. However, if a program satisfies one of the observed conditions, then the execution of this program always terminates in bounded time. In this paper, we present four of these conditions as a first step toward solving the response time analysis problem. An algorithm used to compute upper bounds on the number of recognize-act cycles during the executions of programs with acyclic rule triggering patterns has been developed. We also present an algorithm to compute upper bounds on the numbers of comparisons made by the Rete network during the execution. Furthermore, we show how the proposed algorithms can be applied to a class of programs with cyclic rule-triggering patterns.

We are currently still in the process of implementing the proposed algorithms and evaluating the tightness of the upper bounds obtained. Parts of the algorithms are manually carried out at this time. Therefore, we have not applied the proposed algorithms to a large number of programs.
